item.text: I’m adding only remembered passages that supply a distinct detail or reading absent from the earlier coverage, including wealth lost or transferred, fixed study time, and further uses of the listed cognate roots.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec1/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.11	just balances belong to the Lord	The commentary treats a short measure as a concrete market loss; Proverbs says just balances and weights belong to the Lord. This adds divine ownership to the duty of accurate trade.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.31.6	God weighs the speaker in just scales	The commentary joins deficient scales to a final account; Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity. The verse brings commercial measurement into divine judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.14	wealth lost in a bad venture	The commentary describes trade consuming its principal; Ecclesiastes says wealth can be lost in a bad venture, leaving a father with nothing to pass on. It gives the loss of capital a concrete household consequence.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.15	nothing carried away from toil	The commentary says accumulated wealth cannot outlast a person's time; Ecclesiastes says a person leaves as naked as at birth and takes nothing from toil. It makes the final loss bodily and irreversible.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.5	wealth takes wings	The commentary rejects the belief that wealth can secure a person's future; Proverbs says wealth can suddenly make wings and fly away. It adds an image of capital disappearing beyond its owner's control.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.4	riches fail on the day of wrath	The commentary contrasts a losing trade with the righteous path; Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. It directly contrasts wealth with the return of right conduct.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.1	remember the creator before difficult days	The commentary says a late plea for more time comes after the market has closed; Ecclesiastes urges remembering the creator in youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes the timing of good action urgent.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.32.4	Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ	The commentary glosses amānah as trust opposed to betrayal; Deuteronomy calls God faithful and without injustice. This Hebrew use joins fidelity to justice, though the root correspondence remains unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.15.8	Arabic root خ س ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חסר	The commentary defines loss through diminution and deficiency; Deuteronomy commands opening a hand to a poor person for whatever he lacks (חסר). It connects lack to a neighbor's material need, though cognacy is unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.39.7	Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר	The commentary's Arabic lexical branch calls a ṣubrah a heap sold without weighing; the psalm uses צבר for heaping up wealth and says the person does not know who will gather it. The heap becomes a warning about wealth outliving its owner; cognacy is unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.27.16	Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר	The commentary's lexical branch connects ṣubrah with a heap; Job says the wicked may heap up silver like dust, yet others will wear the garments he prepared. It adds the transfer of accumulated wealth, while the proposed cognacy remains unverified.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.11	faithfulness with money and true riches	The commentary sets trust against betrayal in a commercial setting; Jesus says that failure to be faithful with unrighteous wealth means no one will entrust true riches. It makes money management a test of trustworthiness.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.13	God and wealth as rival masters	The commentary frames the righteous trade as choosing the lasting good over a losing exchange; Jesus says a person cannot serve both God and mammon. It makes wealth a question of allegiance, not merely its amount.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.27	money placed with bankers for interest	The commentary describes capital invested for gain; in the talents parable the master says the servant should have placed the money with bankers so it could return with interest. It makes the expected return explicit.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.21	faithful servant receives greater charge	The commentary connects faithful work to a wage; the master praises a servant faithful over a little, entrusts him with much, and invites him into joy. It adds increased responsibility as the reward for stewardship.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.20.13	agreed denarius as a worker's due	The commentary says a wage is an obligation once due; the vineyard owner answers a complaint by pointing to the agreed denarius. This gives the parable's wage a contractual basis alongside its generosity to later workers.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.6	God rewards those who seek him	The commentary makes belief one condition of escaping loss and describes a later wage; Hebrews says faith is necessary to approach God and that God rewards those who seek him. It joins faith to expected recompense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.10	faithful through death, crowned with life	The commentary couples patience with a wage at the end of the worker's time; Revelation tells Smyrna to remain faithful even to death and promises the crown of life. It makes endurance under threat part of the reward image.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.33	selling goods to give alms and store unfailing treasure	The commentary presents a trade whose return does not fail and recalls a plea for time to give charity; Jesus tells hearers to sell possessions, give to the poor, and provide an unfailing heavenly treasure. It makes generosity a deliberate transfer from perishable wealth.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.19.17	lending to the Lord by helping the poor	The commentary says God is the buyer and guarantor of a promised return; Proverbs says whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the giver. It casts care for the poor as a loan whose return comes from God.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.14.14	repayment at the resurrection	The commentary links righteous deeds to a later wage; Jesus says a host who invites the poor, disabled, lame, and blind will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous. It specifies generosity that cannot be repaid in the present market.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.40	service to the least counted as service to the king	The commentary says mutual counsel must recognize another person's due; in the judgment scene the king identifies care for the least of his siblings as care for himself. It gives acts of service a direct relation to the final judge.
strong	tevrat	motif	Tobit 4:9	alms stored as treasure for a future day	The commentary contrasts wealth that perishes with a trade that does not fail; Tobit says alms lay up a good treasure for the day of need. It makes generosity a future-oriented deposit.
medium	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a	fixed times for Torah study at judgment	The commentary treats a person's time as capital that must be spent before the account closes; Shabbat 31a asks at judgment whether one fixed times for Torah study. This adds deliberate use of time to the passage's separate question about honest business.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Exod.17.12	shared support keeps hands steady until sunset	The commentary joins mutual urging to patience with the end of the workday; Aaron and Hur support Moses' hands until sunset so they remain steady. The scene adds physical, shared endurance through the day's limit.
weak	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.17.12	Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ	The commentary's Arabic lexical gloss associates amānah with trust and firmness; Exodus describes Moses' hands as steady (emunah) until sunset. The Hebrew usage gives the root a bodily sense of sustained firmness, but the sound correspondence is unverified.
EOF"
